title: The craft of controlled surgery
mathematical_role: Orient the reader to controlled surgery on a high-curvature neck and the topological bookkeeping that follows.
learning_objective: Distinguish an S^2 x I neck, cuts along two-spheres, removal of singular ends, and attachment of standard caps from a planar cut-and-paste metaphor.
literal_semantics: The predecessor intends to communicate that a narrow neck is identified before a cut-and-cap operation.
nonliteral_semantics: The planar silhouette is not a literal three-manifold.
The straight cut lines are not literal embedded two-spheres.
The wedge-like endpoints are not standard cap geometry.
No displayed size or shape is a canonical-neighbourhood scale certificate.

notes: Successor must preserve the imported-theorem boundary and must not imply that the visual certifies a surgery event.

reproducibility_notes: The predecessor SVG is preserved by Git blob identity but is not generated from a three-dimensional geometric model.

accessibility.alt_text: A neck-like high-curvature region is cut along controlled spheres and replaced by standard caps.
accessibility.long_description: The current predecessor uses a two-dimensional dumbbell-like outline, cut markers, and wedge-like caps. Those shapes are pedagogical placeholders rather than literal S^2 x I neck geometry, cutting two-spheres, or standard caps. The replacement must show the dimensional and topological structure explicitly.

claim_boundary.strongest_visual_claim: Pedagogical orientation to the sequence identify neck, cut, cap, and continue.
not_claimed: Validity of a specific surgery event
A proof of the Poincare theorem

supersession_reason: The predecessor collapses a three-dimensional neck surgery into planar geometry that can create a materially false mental model.
